newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-ROWELL UNDER PRESSURE TO STAND AND DELIVER.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ROWELL UNDER PRESSURE TO STAND AND DELIVER.

text.p: England have yet to kick, or pass, a ball in this year's Five Nations championship yet discordant drums are already audible at Twickenham even before the Scots cross the border this weekend.

In rugby, as in cricket and soccer and every other sport worthy of the name, there is nothing quite like beating the English which explains why all those appointed to coach or lead England teams soon discover the job is the modern equivalent of being strapped to a water wheel.

Fervent patriots like Graham Taylor, Bobby Robson, Keith Fletcher, David Lloyd and Mike Atherton have all received a ducking and now, unless his slow-burning team suddenly catch fire, it is England rugby coach Jack Rowell's turn to endure the treatment.

Rowell has arguably the finest coaching record at club level in English rugby history and was responsible for Five Nations-winning sides in both his first two seasons, so ripples appeared this week when he was accused of spouting tactical "mumbo-jumbo" to his squad.

What made the story even more piquant was the identity of the man throwing the stones. Geoff Cooke coached and managed England to unprecedented success in the 1980s and 90s and knows precisely what happens when media rottweilers are tossed a juicy bone.

It did not stop him laying into Rowell's management style, criticising him for confusing the players and raising false expectations, although there were subsequent claims only his negative words had been quoted.

Rowell did his best to shrug it all off but Cooke's remarks are not isolated ones. Another former England coach, Dick Best, predicted in November his successor would be sacked in 1997 and the Rugby Football Union were forced to rush out an official denial after a report claimed earlier this month Rowell was on the verge of the chop.

Rowell's success at Bath, where he shared in 16 trophies over 13 years, was based on encouraging players to take responsibility on the field and not allowing even senior team members to settle into a comfort zone.
His problem with England -- and several exist judging by their stuttering display against Argentina last month -- is that few of them seem inclined to grasp the baton.
Rowell has been trying to prise England away from their "relatively static" style of rugby, but now seems to have scaled down his boldest visions of the furtue.

There is no place against Scotland for Jeremy Guscott, Mike Catt, Alex King, Austin Healey or Neil Back, the type of players who might suit an adventurous game, with the steadier Paul Grayson preferred at fly-half and the essentially similar talents of Will Carling and Phil de Glanville still in the centre.
"We could have done for a tour last year for the up-and-comers, to sift and sort," conceded Rowell.
"We have made 10 changes in two years which is a huge amount for any team. We all aspire to win the Five Nations this season, but it depends how fast the people coming in settle down.

"It's just team-building in a big way which England haven't gone through for 10 years or so. Nobody wants it that way, but it's inevitable given the maturity of the team who went into the World Cup in 1995."

There is a growing feeling, though, that England must do more than grind their way through another Five Nations season if they want to threaten the rest of the world, and Rowell would love to recreate the sort of rugby Brive produced in last weekend's European Cup final.

"The players aspire to a more open game and bit by bit we're going to get there. We English are different. We don't have that natural movement. But I think England can nevertheless play dynamically and with flexibility and what we do have is some very mobile forwards. We don't want to be contained into playing anything like 10-man rugby."

Away from rugby, Rowell is a high-powered businessman whose involvement in a number of firms allows him few days off, so it is ironic to hear him complain about spending insufficient time with the England squad in rugby's new professional era.

"Since the Argentina game we've been allowed one training session which ended up as one hour on a semi-frozen pitch in freezing fog. Now, before an international, players have to recover from club matches at a time when you need to invest in some hard work. It's a major issue for England and anyone else whose players are caught up in it."

Such is the pressure on all English coaches these days, time is a commodity which Rowell himself is fast running out of. The next six weeks will determine if his diary is quite as busy this time next year.
